newsitem.title: FRANCE: FOCUS-French industrial production surges in April.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-French industrial production surges in April.

text.p: French industrial production surged in April, lifted mostly by a sharp increase in energy production and more moderate rises in most manufacturing sectors, official figures released on Friday showed.
Overall industrial output was up 3.0 percent, with energy output up 14.8 percent after two straight months of declines, accounting for 1.8 percentage points of the overall rise.
Manufacturing production, which excludes agri-food, energy and construction, rose 1.1 percent in the month, national statistics institute INSEE said.
Economists polled by Reuters on average expected a rise in industrial production of 0.4 percent.
Year-on-year, overall production was up 2.2 percent and manufacturing output rose 3.7 percent, INSEE said.
Economists said the rise, the third consecutive monthly increase in manufacturing output, was good news and hinted that the economy might be picking up steam.

"It's a good report because an increase in 1.1 percent is the sort of increase you just dont get very often and because it comes as the third consecutive monthly rise," said Nomura International bond analyst Sonja Gibbs.
"Ultimately you cannot have such strength in exports without it working through to the domestic economy in some way," she said.

Exports were the driving force of French growth in the first quarter of 1997 and the last three months of 1996, up 1.1 percent and 1.5 percent respectively, and economists said the 12 percent decline in the franc against the dollar so far this year would continue to help exporters.

Economists said France's dependence on exports was highlighted in Friday's industrial production report by the fact sectors depending largely on domestic demand had not seen such large increases in output.
"This number gives a deformed view of the economy," said Herve Goulletquer, economist at Credit Lyonnais. "Without exports, economic growth would not be what it is today."
He said relatively small rises in construction, intermediate goods and capital goods, provided clear evidence that the domestic economy lacked strength.
"The question is whether the manufacturing strength can be spread to other sectors," he said.
Month-on-month, construction output fell 0.7 percent, intermediate goods output was up 0.3 percent and capital goods production rose 1.0 percent.
These numbers compared with a rise in consumer goods production of 2.2 percent and an auto industry increase of 3.5 percent. Agri-food production was up 2.6 percent on the month.

The economy grew 1.5 percent in 1996 and official forecasts predict a 2.3 percent rise this year. Many private economists expect growth to reach barely 2.0 percent unless French companies, wary of the weakness of domestic demand, take the plunge and start investing and restocking inventories.
